William Carey
WIL-yum KAIR-ee
proper noun (figure)
English personal name. William (Germanic, "resolute protector"); Carey, an English surname. William Carey (1761-1834) was a Particular Baptist missionary to India, called the "father of modern missions."

📖 Biblical Definition

William Carey (1761-1834) was the Particular Baptist cobbler-turned-missionary whose vision and labor made him the father of the modern Protestant missionary movement. A self-educated shoemaker who taught himself Latin, Greek, Hebrew, and several other languages while mending shoes, Carey was gripped by the unreached nations and wrote his epoch-making An Enquiry into the Obligations of Christians to Use Means for the Conversion of the Heathens (1792), which demolished the hyper-Calvinist objection that the Great Commission was binding only on the apostles. His famous sermon on Isaiah 54:2-3 issued the watchword of the movement: "Expect great things from God; attempt great things for God." That year, with Andrew Fuller and others, he founded the Baptist Missionary Society and sailed for India in 1793. He spent forty-one years there without a furlough, settling at Serampore, where he and his colleagues (the "Serampore Trio" with Joshua Marshman and William Ward) translated the Scriptures, in whole or part, into dozens of Indian languages and dialects, established schools and a college, fought the practice of widow-burning (sati), and labored against caste injustice. Carey buried a son and watched his first wife descend into mental illness; he pressed on. His combination of definite-atonement Calvinism, linguistic genius, and dogged perseverance set the pattern for two centuries of Protestant missions. The doctrines of grace did not freeze his zeal; they fueled it.

WILLIAM CAREY, proper noun. English Particular Baptist missionary (1761-1834).

Self-educated cobbler who taught himself Latin, Greek, Hebrew, and more while mending shoes.

Author of the Enquiry (1792); preached "Expect great things from God; attempt great things for God."

Co-founded the Baptist Missionary Society (1792); sailed for India 1793; 41 years at Serampore without furlough.

Translated Scripture into dozens of Indian languages; fought sati and caste injustice; called the father of modern missions.

⚠️ Modern Corruption

William Carey is corrupted when reduced to a motivational slogan, when his missionary labor is severed from his Calvinistic theology, or when modern missiology claims his name while abandoning the gospel of definite atonement and conversion that drove him.

expand to see more

Slogan-reduction. Carey is widely known for one sentence — "Expect great things from God; attempt great things for God" — lifted from its sermon and printed on conference banners. The slogan is true, but the man behind it was a definite-atonement Calvinist, a translator of staggering discipline, and a sufferer who buried a child and bore a wife's madness across decades in a foreign land. To keep the slogan and lose the theology, the discipline, and the suffering is to keep the poster and lose the missionary.

Gospel-severed missiology. Modern missiology sometimes invokes Carey's name while redefining the missionary task away from conversion and toward social transformation, interfaith dialogue, or development work alone. Carey did fight sati and caste injustice — but as the overflow of a gospel that called individual sinners to repentance and faith in Christ, and that drove him to translate the Scriptures so that they could read the call for themselves. His social reform flowed from gospel conversion; it did not replace it. The dictionary honors the whole Carey: the converting gospel first, the social fruit following.
